description.summary: Redis is an in-memory data platform with native exact, approximate, filtered, full-text, and hybrid vector retrieval over hash and JSON documents.
description.description: Redis combines its low-latency in-memory data structures with secondary indexing, full-text search, geospatial and metadata filtering, and vector retrieval. Redis 8 supports FLAT, HNSW, and SVS-VAMANA vector indexes, KNN and range queries, and FT.HYBRID fusion of text and vector results. Redis can run locally or self-hosted, scale through Redis Cluster and asynchronous replication, or be consumed as Redis Cloud. This record separates in-memory query performance from persistence durability, replication consistency, cluster behavior, managed-service guarantees, and workload-specific vector recall.

indexingConsiderations: Select FLAT, HNSW, or SVS-VAMANA only after measuring recall, latency, memory, construction time, compression, and hardware behavior on representative vectors.
Size memory for primary data, secondary indexes, replication buffers, persistence copy-on-write overhead, client buffers, and operational headroom.
Use explicit HASH or JSON schemas, vector dimensions, element types, distance metrics, key prefixes, and indexed metadata fields.
Plan Redis Cluster hash slots, shard count, replica count, hot-key distribution, persistence, and failover capacity before large-scale ingestion.
retrievalConsiderations: Evaluate text-only, vector-only, and FT.HYBRID retrieval on the same relevance set before choosing RRF or linear fusion.
Tune EF_RUNTIME, KNN candidate counts, SHARD_K_RATIO, filter policy, batch size, fusion windows, rank constants, and weights under representative load.
Distinguish vector pre-filters from post-combination filters because they change candidate eligibility, result counts, and latency.
Account for key expiration, eviction policy, replication lag, failover, and persistence when Redis is used as the authoritative RAG memory store.

limitations: Vector indexes and primary data consume memory, so dataset size, index overhead, fragmentation, replicas, and persistence forks must be capacity-planned together.
SVS-VAMANA compression behavior and proprietary Intel optimizations depend on hardware, build options, platform, and selected Redis license.
Redis replication is asynchronous by default, and acknowledged writes can still be lost during failover depending on persistence and topology.
Redis Cluster supports atomic multi-key operations only when the participating keys are colocated in the same hash slot.
MULTI/EXEC serializes queued commands but does not roll back successful commands when another queued command fails during execution.
RDB, AOF, and combined persistence trade restart time, write amplification, latency, storage, and possible data loss differently.
FT.HYBRID fusion and filtered vector retrieval require workload-specific relevance, latency, memory, and cluster evaluation.
Redis 8 uses a tri-license choice of RSALv2, SSPLv1, or AGPLv3, and optional proprietary vector optimizations can impose additional compatibility constraints.
usageGuidance: Record the Redis server, client, query-engine, and index versions because vector types, algorithms, defaults, commands, and cluster behavior evolve across releases.
Use Redis primarily when low-latency mutable retrieval, caching, session memory, or real-time data structures justify the in-memory cost model.
Benchmark the complete RAG workload including ingestion, expiration, filters, hybrid fusion, replication, persistence, failover, and recovery.
Use ACLs, TLS, network isolation, key-prefix conventions, and deployment-specific tenant controls rather than exposing Redis directly to untrusted clients.
Test RDB and AOF recovery, replica promotion, cluster resharding, memory pressure, and eviction behavior before production adoption.

references.title: Redis Documentation: Scale with Redis Cluster

claims.statement: Redis stores vectors and metadata in hashes or JSON documents and supports exact FLAT search, approximate HNSW search, and SVS-VAMANA graph search with optional compression across cosine, inner-product, and Euclidean distance metrics.
claims.rationale: The Redis repository, release, Search overview, and vector documentation describe Redis as a vector-capable in-memory data platform and enumerate its storage models, vector index families, compression options, and metrics.

claims.statement: Redis supports metadata-aware vector retrieval using exact-match, numeric-range, full-text, geospatial, and logical pre-filters, with runtime heuristics or explicit ADHOC_BF and BATCHES policies for filtered KNN execution.

qualifiers.name: filterScope
qualifiers.value: Filter behavior depends on query dialect, index type, selectivity, cluster topology, and the selected hybrid policy

claims.rationale: The vector and combined-query documentation describes structured filters before KNN search and documents the execution policies used to balance brute-force filtering against batched ANN traversal.

claims.statement: Redis FT.HYBRID combines BM25-style text search and vector similarity in one query and supports Reciprocal Rank Fusion or weighted linear fusion, vector pre-filtering, post-combination filtering, and cluster candidate controls.

qualifiers.name: availabilityScope
qualifiers.value: FT.HYBRID is available from Redis Open Source 8.4 and Redis 8.8 adds shard-candidate and profiling improvements

claims.rationale: The Redis 8.8 release and FT.HYBRID command reference document unified text-vector retrieval, RRF and linear fusion, filter placement, candidate windows, shard controls, and profiling support.

claims.statement: Redis Cluster horizontally shards keys across nodes, Redis replication uses asynchronous leader-follower propagation with optional WAIT acknowledgements, and Redis Cloud provides a managed service with scaling, failover, backup, and recovery capabilities.

qualifiers.name: deploymentScope
qualifiers.value: Self-hosted Redis Open Source, Redis Cluster, and Redis Cloud expose different operational guarantees and responsibility boundaries

claims.rationale: Official deployment documentation describes automatic key sharding, replica promotion and migration, asynchronous replication semantics, and the managed Redis Cloud operating model.

claims.statement: Redis provides configurable RDB snapshots, append-only-file logging, or combined persistence and supports serialized MULTI/EXEC transactions with WATCH-based optimistic locking, but transaction errors are not rolled back and durability depends on persistence and replication configuration.

qualifiers.name: durabilityScope
qualifiers.value: RDB intervals, AOF fsync policy, failover, replication lag, and transaction error handling determine effective durability and atomicity

claims.rationale: Redis persistence and transaction documentation distinguishes snapshots from command logging and documents transaction serialization, optimistic locking, partial command errors, and the absence of relational rollback semantics.

evidence.summary: Redis official sources list HASH and JSON vector storage, FLAT, HNSW, and SVS-VAMANA indexes, L2, inner-product, and cosine metrics, and multiple numeric vector encodings and compression modes.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can classify Redis as an in-memory vector store with exact, graph-based ANN, and compressed vector-search options rather than as a dedicated disk-first vector database.

sourceFragments.locator: Repository description, licensing, and vector-query engine overview
Redis Search capabilities and use cases
Vector index algorithms, storage types, metrics, and compression

limitations: Official project documentation is not an independent performance benchmark.
FLAT, HNSW, and SVS-VAMANA have different recall, latency, memory, training, hardware, and build-time tradeoffs.

evidence.summary: Redis documents exact, range, text, geospatial, and logical filters before vector search and dynamically chooses between batched ANN traversal and ad-hoc brute-force evaluation.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark pre-filtered vector retrieval while warning that filter selectivity and execution policy materially influence latency and candidate completeness.

sourceFragments.locator: Filtered vector search, HYBRID_POLICY, BATCHES, and ADHOC_BF
Combined-query operators and KNN pre-filter syntax

limitations: Highly selective or complex filters can change the chosen execution strategy and latency profile.
Cluster candidate ratios and uneven shard distributions can return fewer than the requested top-k results.

evidence.summary: FT.HYBRID exposes text search, vector KNN or range retrieval, BM25 scoring, RRF or linear fusion, filter placement, shard candidate controls, and query profiling.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can represent native lexical-vector hybrid retrieval and configurable fusion without claiming that one fusion method or weight setting is universally optimal.

sourceFragments.locator: Redis 8.8 FT.HYBRID shard-candidate and profiling enhancements
FT.HYBRID syntax, fusion, filtering, defaults, and complexity

limitations: RRF windows, rank constants, linear weights, KNN candidates, and filters require relevance and latency evaluation.
Linear fusion combines heterogeneous score domains and should be validated against the target data and scorer configuration.

evidence.summary: Redis Cluster automatically shards data, replicas can be promoted after failures, replication is asynchronous by default, and Redis Cloud provides managed scaling and recovery features.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark high horizontal scalability and replication while using configurable consistency rather than claiming globally strong consistency under failover.

sourceFragments.locator: Redis Cluster sharding, failover, and replica migration
Asynchronous replication, WAIT, and failover limitations
Managed service, scalability, failover, backups, and recovery

limitations: WAIT reduces risk but does not turn Redis replication into a strongly consistent CP system.
Cluster slot layout, replica count, failover timing, hot keys, and managed-service limits affect resilience and performance.

evidence.summary: Redis supports RDB, AOF, combined persistence, and no-persistence modes, while MULTI/EXEC serializes queued commands and WATCH provides optimistic concurrency control.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark limited transactional support and configurable durability while distinguishing command serialization from rollback-capable relational transactions.

sourceFragments.locator: RDB, AOF, combined persistence, fsync, backup, and recovery tradeoffs
MULTI, EXEC, DISCARD, WATCH, serialization, and error semantics

limitations: RDB can lose writes since the last snapshot and AOF durability depends on fsync policy and file integrity.
Commands that fail after EXEC do not roll back other successfully executed commands.
